text: An orbit that goes around the Earth 8.05 times a day with an eccentricity of 0.25 (the exact 8:1 resonance with the Earth's rotation) is predicted 1.3 km off along its track 7 days after a fit, against 94 to 220 m just either side of it: no part of the model carries that resonance's gravity terms.

On seven real windows of the TESS space telescope (an orbit of 13.7 days that reaches the Moon's distance), predictions from 72-hour fits are a median 1.01 km off after one day, 2.0 km after three days and 9.0 km after a week. The test holds them to the archived 0.77 km at one day and 7.6 km at a week, and to no more than 50 m behind SGP4-XP at three days, where they are 706 m behind. The numerical propagator, fitted and scored the same way, is 0.48, 1.57 and 11.5 km off. The cause is AP's radiation pressure on that orbit: a 72-hour fit follows the numerical propagator's radiation pressure no closer than 46 to 174 m, and misses it by 1.5 to 7 km five days later. With every force but radiation pressure, AP follows the numerical propagator to within 37 m over a week.

On a 7-day arc of an eccentric orbit with drag (Molniya), the record states the drag coefficient to 0.09 % while the fitted value is 0.3 to 0.5 % from the truth: the stated uncertainty is 5 to 7 times too small; its position covariance is honest.
